game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

It has several different endings, which are well-implemented, but the circumstances of the ending's gameplay were so muddled for me that I accidentally clicked my way into an ending I didn't want because I wasn't sure how to do what I wanted to do and I was loaded down with so much unprocessed information I had had to leave for later. The fact that the game jumps at the opportunity to end instead of letting you log out on your own terms when you've done what you want to do doesn't help. This critique probably makes more sense to those who have played it.

All in all, it's a brilliant little dystopia simulator with a lot of love and care poured into it, and a very pleasant and thought-provoking experience I highly recommend. Like any creation, it has its flaws, but it's well worth the price and you can tell how much work went into it.

Pretty crappy thing to do for anybody playing the game more than once, (or for somebody playing your game for the third time just to get the Achievement Endings).

Great. Decided to check it absolutely randomly, when my main PC was in repair and I was looking for something simple for my working laptop. Honestly, never thought that it is possible to create an interesting story and gameplay... just from reading messages, chat and newspaper articles. Your actions have consequences and you decide how the story goes and how will it end. And yeah, it has some replay value.

Thus, in most cases I don't even bother to check it and just play in English. However, the game offered me to play in my language right away, so I decided to give it a chance. And the quality in indeed great. If indie studio is capable to do it, it's even more pathetic when big and greedy studios and their shills often find numerous excuses not to translate their games into more languages.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]”An interactive dystopian detective novel at its best”[/b]
 
[h1]The Good[/h1]
 
Orwell is an electrifying, Orwellian, (surprisingly enough) thriller with exciting twists and turns everywhere you look. The varied choices and the believable medium through which they are presented breathe so much life into the world and its characters. The mechanics, while there aren’t many to play with and master, they are polished and intuitive enough to get the point across in a believable manner. The writing and world building have to carry the game almost entirely and I can gladly say Osmotic Studios has delivered in this regard! Further to add to this, the pacing fits well into a fairly short experience, around 4 hours, which allows for easy and frequent replayability.
The choices you make are integral to the twists and turns you take. The way the choices are handled in Orwell are often left ambiguous with their outcome and effect on the world around you. Even then, every choice you make feels as though it has an impact on the world, no matter how small.
 
[h1]The Bad[/h1]
 
Certain aspects of the game can fell sluggish, such as the tiresome phone call logs and the constant (seemingly) dead ends on web pages. There can be a case made for these moments, however, since they do add to the overall integrity of this fictional world. My only fear is that some players may feel a bit disappointed during these moments that are paced so much slower than the bits in which the player is in direct control.
Another personal gripe with this game is that it’s cast, and plot can feel too expansive given the short time period the game takes place over. Certain events can completely go over the player’s head what with so many people and connections to remember.
 
[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
 
Orwell is an excellent example of compelling and effective storytelling told through the interactive medium of video games. It’s easy to get into and while it may not be the easiest narrative to understand, the writing will keep you engaged constantly. However, at times the story does slow down, and it is easy to get fatigued with the sheer amount of writing in this game.
I think it’s easiest to sum up Orwell as an interactive, dystopian, detective novel at its best. In a game that hinges on the “choices matter” idea, it does well in treating the player like an intelligent and competent participant. You have the ability to make inferences that might not accomplish what you’re trying to do. Also, it is important to note that in a game whose themes are centered around a battling of ideals the player’s choices are remarked upon by all characters and it is easy to let your biases make choices for you. I really do recommend this game to those of you that are itching to fit into the shoes of a detective that is a 3rd party in a war of ideals. Be careful with those choices of yours though, you never know who’s watching.
 
[h1]8/10[/h1]

Also, it is important to note that in a game whose themes are centered around a battling of ideals the player’s choices are remarked upon by all characters and it is easy to let your biases make choices for you. I really do recommend this game to those of you that are itching to fit into the shoes of a detective that is a 3rd party in a war of ideals. Be careful with those choices of yours though, you never know who’s watching. [h1]8/10[/h1]

...But ideas, ideas are bullet-proof.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is... Well, it's different.
I understand that some people have their objections against it but it's interesting. At first you start it as any "adventure" game and focus on simply picking up information (and think this game is silly because it all boils down to simply pulling highlited items from one window to another; ok, it's got a story but that's as much "interactive" as it gets).
Then you notice that you get to chose not only which of conflicting parts of data you pass on to the system, but also how many of them you decide to omit.
Then you notice that your choices do have an impact on the story and how it unfolds.
Of course, you may treat this as a manifesto against surveilance but can also treat it as an interesting experiment in balancing the needs of the many with the needs of ones. And a study about security and privacy. And your own approach. Because the more you get involved with the story, the more interesting it gets.
The only flaw I see is that you can't manually save and revert to a point in time to make different choice and see its result. I can understand why it was done this way but since you'd need to play the game from the very beginning, the game loses its replayability value.
I probably wouldn't buy this game for its full price but I'm glad I played it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Ugh. So this is one of those games I wish Steam had a 'meh' review button for.

It started off strong. I really was hooked on my first playthrough. The concept is neat - you really feel like you're in charge of what information gets through and what doesn't. It took me about 3 hours (with reading everything) to get to the end my first time around. I was very disappointed it was so short - primarily because I honestly thought that there was going to be more than one case to investigate. Yeah - not the case.

Since I'm an achievement whore, I started another run through. This is where the game completely fails. It has, in my opinion, very little replay value. You start to learn that your choices don't actually do much to effect the outcome of the game. You can sort of control what happens to each person based on the information you submit, and occasionally certain things only unlock with certain choices....but other than that the dialogue is very very similar throughout. There is no fastforward button (that I could find) and no back button in case you screw up, which means you would have to completely start over if you mess up a chain of events to get a specific achievement.

It took two more playthroughs (three total) of two and a half hours each (aqain, can't skip ANY dialogue) to finish all achievements (gameplay time is a little higher because I would leave it running while doing other things). I was literally not at all invested in the game at this point because the changes in dialogue/direction are so small that they reduce replay value to nill.

I'm glad I got the game on sale because it's not worth $10, considering how short it is and how little replay value there is due to limitation of choice.

I dunno - the concept is unique and it was fun to play the first time around, so I do recommend it if you're looking for something intriguing to play on a rainy day. But I recommend getting it on sale.
